evidence_quotes.quote: Using the Aquastat database, water consumption in the world and water availability in LAC were studied. In addition, the regulatory framework for water in LAC countries was studied, with an emphasis on water reuse and greywater legislation.
In addition, the political constitution of several LAC countries was exhaustively reviewed, particularly, water laws.

The economic indicators presented in this paper were obtained from the World Bank database. The data collected from the different databases were analyzed and correlated with each other. In addition, ArcGIS software was used for the analysis and graphing of the results.
In LAC, only Chile has a legal norm on the specific matter of greywater, recognizing its separation from black water and therefore, from the general regulation of sanitation.
Figure 5 shows the relationship between Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per capita and access to healthy drinking water in some countries in Latin America.

The contribution of this work is that it presented a general overview of the management of water resources in the region, emphasizing the potential of greywater reuse and including a review of technological and economic aspects.

criterion_notes.c1: Although the review focuses primarily on water resource distribution, agricultural water demand and the prospects for wastewater reclamation and household greywater reuse, Sections 4 and 7.2 descriptively review country-level urban and rural drinking-water access coverage and household water tariffs across Latin America and the Caribbean.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper examines legal and regulatory factors by cataloging constitutional right-to-water provisions, national water resource laws, wastewater reuse standards and greywater reuse legislation/bills (Section 7, Tables 2 and 3) and narratively discussing privatization vs. public/community management (Section 8). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is NO: the specific regulatory analysis centers on environmental/technical standards for agricultural wastewater reclamation and decentralized greywater reuse rather than a rule-type mechanism governing household water or sanitation service access, while general water laws, constitutional clauses, tariffs and privatization are treated only as unanalysed macro-governance background. Note that even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper is still excluded (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because it fails Criteria 3 and 5 as a non-systematic narrative and doctrinal overview without empirical analysis linking any legal or regulatory factor to service access.
criterion_notes.c3: NO (E05): This is a narrative literature and policy/regulatory review (using an unstructured Google Scholar keyword search without systematic review methods, eligibility gates or synthesis protocol) combined with descriptive background charts of country-level FAO AQUASTAT water indicators and World Bank GDP per capita. It contains no primary empirical data, no systematic empirical synthesis and no empirical analysis testing any legal, administrative or governance factor in relation to water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c4: Sections 4 and 7.2 report descriptive secondary statistics from FAO AQUASTAT and utility tariff schedules on national population coverage of healthy drinking water (total, urban and rural) and average household water prices for 30 m3/month, though only as macro-level context and bivariate scatterplots against GDP per capita.
criterion_notes.c5: NO: Because the paper is a narrative review and descriptive regulatory compilation, there is no identifiable empirical study design or analytical exposure-outcome structure linking a legal, regulatory or administrative exposure to household or community service access.

study_design: Narrative literature and regulatory review with descriptive secondary macro-indicator compilation
country: Latin America and the Caribbean (regional overview including Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay and Venezuela)
population_and_sample: Countries in Latin America and the Caribbean (national-level FAO AQUASTAT water resource and access indicators, World Bank GDP per capita, utility water rates and national water legislation)
exposure: not reported (descriptive compilation of constitutional water provisions, general water laws and wastewater/greywater reuse legislation; not empirically tested as an exposure)
outcome: Descriptive country-level percentage of population with access to healthy drinking water (total, urban and rural) and household water price for 30 m3/month from secondary databases
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Rodríguez et al. (2022) present a narrative literature and regulatory review of water resource distribution, wastewater reclamation and greywater reuse prospects across Latin America and the Caribbean. While the paper descriptively plots country-level FAO AQUASTAT drinking-water coverage and household water prices against World Bank GDP per capita and inventories constitutional water clauses, general water laws and greywater reuse bills/statutes, it is neither an empirical study testing a legal/administrative mechanism on service access nor a systematic empirical synthesis. It also fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because its regulatory focus is technical/environmental greywater and agricultural wastewater reuse legislation, with general water governance discussed only as unanalysed macro-level background; under the plain wording of Criterion 2 it would likewise be excluded for lack of empirical access-governance evidence and lack of an identifiable exposure-outcome empirical design.
